clinicalPearls: A generally benign autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia associated with heterozygous (monoallelic) mutations in GP1BA, part of the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex
Represents the heterozygous carrier state of Bernard-Soulier syndrome, whose biallelic form is far more severe
Characterised by mild thrombocytopenia with large platelets and usually little or no bleeding tendency
Often discovered incidentally on a routine full blood count or misclassified by automated analysers that miscount giant platelets
Platelet aggregation to ristocetin may be mildly reduced but is far less abnormal than in biallelic Bernard-Soulier syndrome
Recognition prevents inappropriate treatment for presumed immune thrombocytopenia
It is particularly described in Mediterranean populations, hence the name
Diagnosis rests on film review of platelet morphology, flow cytometry of GPIb, and GP1BA genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: GP1BA encodes GPIb-alpha, a subunit of the platelet GPIb-IX-V receptor complex that binds von Willebrand factor and mediates platelet adhesion. In the biallelic state, loss of the complex causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome with giant platelets and severe bleeding. A single mutant allele (monoallelic) produces a milder phenotype in which platelet production and size regulation are partially disturbed, giving mild macrothrombocytopenia with largely preserved haemostatic function. The enlarged platelets and modestly reduced counts reflect abnormal megakaryocyte fragmentation rather than peripheral destruction.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited macrothrombocytopenias (for example GP9, GP1BB variants)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with manual film review to confirm large platelets and exclude clumping
Flow cytometry for GPIb-IX-V complex expression
Family studies given autosomal dominant inheritance
Exclusion of secondary and immune causes of thrombocytopenia
redFlags: Bleeding that is more severe than expected, prompting reassessment for biallelic Bernard-Soulier syndrome or an additional disorder
Progressive fall in platelet count suggesting a superimposed acquired process
Additional cytopenias or systemic features indicating another diagnosis
Marked haemorrhage during surgery or trauma requiring platelet support
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually benign with a normal life expectancy and minimal bleeding, and its main clinical importance lies in correct recognition to avoid unnecessary investigation and treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as immune thrombocytopenia leading to steroids, immunoglobulin, or splenectomy
Accepting a falsely low automated platelet count when giant platelets are miscounted
Confusing the mild heterozygous phenotype with severe biallelic Bernard-Soulier syndrome
Overlooking pseudothrombocytopenia from in-vitro platelet clumping
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
